course.title: Comparative Government & Politics
course.description: A tour of how governments are built and how they differ, from states and constitutions to elections, parties, and political change, using real examples from the United States, United Kingdom, Germany, France, China, and more. Topic framing is adapted from the Comparative politics article on Wikipedia, the free encyclopedia (CC BY-SA 4.0). The prose here is original and written to be accurate and non-partisan.

questions.prompt: Comparative politics is best described as the study of...
options: treaties and war between sovereign states
political systems compared across different countries
the legal history of one country
questions.explanation: Comparative politics compares institutions and processes across countries; relations between states is the separate field of international relations.

questions.prompt: Sovereignty most precisely means...
options: the right to vote in elections
supreme authority over a territory and its people
questions.explanation: Sovereignty is a state's claim to final authority within its borders - see 'The state, sovereignty, and legitimacy'.

questions.prompt: A hallmark that distinguishes a democracy from an authoritarian regime is...
options: regular, competitive elections with real uncertainty about who wins
questions.explanation: Many regimes have constitutions and armies; genuine competitive elections are the defining democratic feature.

questions.prompt: In a parliamentary system such as the United Kingdom's, the head of government is...
options: directly elected by voters in a separate national ballot
chosen by and accountable to the legislature
questions.explanation: A prime minister comes from the legislature and holds office only while commanding its confidence.

questions.prompt: First-past-the-post (single-member plurality) elections tend to produce...
options: a system dominated by two large parties
questions.explanation: Plurality rules reward the largest party in each district and squeeze out smaller ones, nudging toward two-party competition.

questions.prompt: A federal state, such as Germany or the United States, is one in which...
options: all power rests with the national government
power is constitutionally divided between national and regional governments
regions may leave whenever they wish
questions.explanation: Federalism entrenches a division of powers between central and regional levels that neither can abolish alone.

questions.prompt: The phrase 'rule of law' means above all that...
options: the government may act however it wishes
everyone, including those who govern, is bound by known law
questions.explanation: The rule of law subjects rulers and ruled alike to public, stable rules applied by independent courts.

questions.prompt: 'Democratization' refers to...
options: a country moving from more authoritarian to more democratic rule
the writing of a new national anthem
questions.explanation: Democratization is the transition toward competitive, accountable government - see 'Political economy and political change'.

lessons.title: The state, sovereignty, and legitimacy
lessons.grammar_note: Keep 'state', 'government', and 'nation' distinct: the state is the lasting legal structure, the government is the team currently running it, and a nation is a people who feel they belong together.

sections.heading: What you'll be able to do
sections.text: After this lesson you can explain what comparative politics studies, define the state, and distinguish sovereignty from legitimacy. You will also see why we compare countries at all. Warm-up from the diagnostic: in one sentence, how does comparative politics differ from international relations?

sections.heading: The idea
sections.text: Comparative politics is the branch of political science that compares how different countries organize and exercise power. Rather than studying relations between states, which is international relations, it looks inside states to ask how institutions, elections, parties, and policies work and why they vary. The central object is the state: the lasting set of institutions that claims a monopoly on the legitimate use of force within a defined territory, a formulation associated with the sociologist Max Weber. Three ideas recur. Sovereignty is the claim to supreme authority within borders, so that no outside power and no internal rival may override it. Legitimacy is the belief, held widely enough by the governed, that the rulers have the right to rule; without it, obedience must rest on force alone. The government, by contrast, is simply the particular set of office-holders running the state at a given moment. We compare countries to test explanations: if two states differ in outcome, comparing their institutions helps reveal what made the difference.

sections.heading: Concepts and country examples
sections.text: Weber identified three bases of legitimacy. Traditional legitimacy rests on long custom, as with the hereditary monarchies of the United Kingdom or Japan, where the crown endures while elected governments come and go. Charismatic legitimacy rests on devotion to a single leader. Legal-rational legitimacy rests on impersonal rules and offices, the dominant form in modern states such as Germany or France, where authority attaches to the office, not the person. Sovereignty can be internal, meaning final authority at home, and external, meaning recognition by other states. The United States and China both assert full sovereignty yet organize power very differently inside their borders. Comparativists use methods too: a most-similar design compares countries that are alike except for one factor, while a most-different design looks for a shared outcome across otherwise dissimilar cases. These designs turn description into explanation.

sections.heading: Your turn
sections.text: 1) Name Weber's three sources of legitimacy. 2) Is 'the current prime minister resigned' a statement about the state or the government? 3) What is the difference between internal and external sovereignty? 4) Give one example of traditional legitimacy. 5) Why might a government with elections still lack legitimacy for some citizens? Answers: 1) traditional, charismatic, legal-rational. 2) the government, since the state continues. 3) internal is final authority at home; external is recognition by other states. 4) a hereditary monarchy such as the United Kingdom or Japan. 5) if people doubt the elections were fair or free, belief in the right to rule can erode.

sections.heading: Common mistakes and exit ticket
sections.text: Mistake: treating 'state' and 'government' as synonyms; the government changes while the state persists. Mistake: assuming legitimacy and legality are the same; an action can be legal yet widely seen as illegitimate, or vice versa. Exit ticket: (a) Define sovereignty in one line. (b) Which basis of legitimacy rests on impersonal rules and offices? Answers: sovereignty is the claim to supreme authority within a territory; legal-rational legitimacy.

lessons.title: Types of government and measuring democracy
lessons.grammar_note: Authoritarian and totalitarian are not interchangeable: all totalitarian regimes are authoritarian, but most authoritarian regimes are not totalitarian because they do not try to control everything.

sections.heading: What you'll be able to do
sections.text: You will be able to tell democracy, authoritarianism, and totalitarianism apart, place real regimes on that spectrum, and explain how scholars try to measure how democratic a country is. Warm-up: what single feature most clearly separates a democracy from an authoritarian state?

sections.heading: The idea
sections.text: Governments are often sorted by how power is won and how far it reaches. A democracy selects rulers through regular, competitive elections in which the outcome is genuinely uncertain, and it protects the civil liberties, free press, and rule of law that make such competition meaningful. An authoritarian regime concentrates power in a leader or party and limits or manipulates competition, but it usually leaves large parts of private life alone. A totalitarian regime goes further: it seeks total control of politics, the economy, and even thought, backed by an official ideology, a single mass party, and pervasive surveillance. Between clear democracies and clear autocracies lies a wide band of hybrid regimes, sometimes called competitive authoritarian, which hold elections that are real but tilted so the rulers rarely lose. Measuring where a country sits is hard, so researchers build indices from many indicators rather than relying on a single yes-or-no label.

sections.heading: Concepts and country examples
sections.text: The United States, Germany, France, India, and the United Kingdom are generally classified as democracies, though each has its own flaws and debates. China is a one-party authoritarian state led by the Communist Party of China, with no competitive national elections. The clearest historical cases of totalitarianism are Nazi Germany and the Soviet Union under Stalin, which combined one ruling party, an official ideology, and mass terror. Several projects try to measure democracy on a scale. Freedom House rates political rights and civil liberties; the Polity project scores regimes from autocracy to democracy; the Varieties of Democracy (V-Dem) project uses thousands of expert-coded indicators; and the Economist Democracy Index ranks countries into categories from full democracy to authoritarian. These measures often agree on clear cases and disagree on the gray zone, which is itself informative. None is neutral or final, so careful analysts report several.

sections.heading: Your turn
sections.text: 1) What distinguishes a totalitarian regime from an ordinary authoritarian one? 2) Name two projects that measure democracy. 3) Is a country with elections automatically a democracy? 4) Which party governs China? 5) What is a hybrid or competitive authoritarian regime? Answers: 1) the totalitarian regime tries to control nearly all of life, guided by an official ideology and a single mass party. 2) any two of Freedom House, Polity, V-Dem, and the Economist Democracy Index. 3) no, if the elections are not free, fair, or competitive. 4) the Communist Party of China. 5) one that holds real elections that are so skewed the incumbents almost always win.

sections.heading: Common mistakes and exit ticket
sections.text: Mistake: calling every harsh government totalitarian; the word has a precise meaning tied to total control and ideology. Mistake: assuming a single index is the truth; indices are estimates that reasonable methods can disagree about. Exit ticket: (a) Name the defining feature of a democracy. (b) Give one reason scholars prefer several democracy measures over one. Answers: regular, free, and competitive elections with protected liberties; because measurement is uncertain and comparing indices reveals where that uncertainty lies.

lessons.title: Constitutions, the rule of law, and federalism
lessons.grammar_note: A constitution can be codified (written in one document, as in the United States) or uncodified (spread across many sources, as in the United Kingdom); 'unwritten' is a loose label, since even the United Kingdom's rules are mostly written down.

sections.heading: What you'll be able to do
sections.text: You will be able to explain what a constitution does, state what the rule of law requires, and contrast federal with unitary states using real examples. Warm-up: how can the United Kingdom be said to have a constitution if it has no single constitutional document?

sections.heading: The idea
sections.text: A constitution is the basic framework that establishes the institutions of the state, distributes power among them, and sets limits on what the government may do. Most countries have a codified constitution in a single written document; the United Kingdom is the famous exception, with an uncodified constitution built from statutes, court decisions, and long-standing conventions. The rule of law is the principle that government itself is bound by public, stable, and fairly applied rules, enforced by independent courts, so that no one is above the law. A related choice is how power is divided by territory. In a unitary state, ultimate authority rests with the national government, which may create or dissolve lower units. In a federal state, a constitution guarantees regional governments their own sphere of authority that the center cannot simply abolish. The difference shapes everything from taxation to schooling.

sections.heading: Concepts and country examples
sections.text: The United States has a short codified constitution (1787) with judicial review, under which courts may strike down laws that conflict with it. Germany's Basic Law (Grundgesetz, 1949) protects core rights so strongly that some cannot be amended at all, a clause known as the eternity guarantee. France's current constitution dates to 1958 and the Fifth Republic. On territory, the United States, Germany, India, and Switzerland are federations: American states, German Lander, and Swiss cantons hold constitutionally protected powers. France is a classic unitary state, with most authority flowing from Paris. The United Kingdom is traditionally unitary but has devolved powers to Scotland, Wales, and Northern Ireland, an arrangement that is not full federalism because Parliament retains the right, in principle, to reclaim those powers. These structures determine where decisions are made and who can block them.

sections.heading: Your turn
sections.text: 1) What is the difference between a codified and an uncodified constitution? 2) What does judicial review allow courts to do? 3) In a unitary state, where does ultimate authority rest? 4) Name two federal countries. 5) Is United Kingdom devolution the same as federalism? Answers: 1) a codified constitution is one written document; an uncodified one is spread across statutes, rulings, and conventions. 2) strike down laws that conflict with the constitution. 3) with the national government. 4) any two of the United States, Germany, India, Switzerland. 5) no, because Parliament can in principle reclaim the devolved powers, so they are not constitutionally guaranteed.

sections.heading: Common mistakes and exit ticket
sections.text: Mistake: saying the United Kingdom has no constitution; it has one, just not in a single codified document. Mistake: confusing federalism with mere decentralization; federalism entrenches regional powers against the center. Exit ticket: (a) State the core idea of the rule of law. (b) Name the key difference between unitary and federal states. Answers: government and governed alike are bound by known, independently enforced law; in a federation regional powers are constitutionally protected, while in a unitary state the center holds ultimate authority.

questions.prompt: Weber's definition of the state centers on a monopoly over...
options: the legitimate use of force within a territory
questions.explanation: The state claims the sole right to the legitimate use of force inside its borders.

questions.prompt: Legal-rational legitimacy rests on...
options: devotion to a single charismatic leader
impersonal rules and the authority of office
questions.explanation: Legal-rational authority attaches to offices and rules, not persons - the dominant modern form.

questions.prompt: Which set of countries is generally classified as democracies?
options: China and the Soviet Union under Stalin
questions.explanation: Germany, France, and India hold regular competitive elections with protected liberties.

questions.prompt: A totalitarian regime differs from an authoritarian one mainly because it...
options: seeks near-total control of society guided by an official ideology
questions.explanation: Totalitarianism aims at total control plus an official ideology, going well beyond ordinary authoritarian rule.

questions.prompt: Judicial review is the power of courts to...
options: strike down laws that conflict with the constitution
questions.explanation: Judicial review lets courts invalidate laws incompatible with the constitution, as in the United States.

questions.prompt: The United Kingdom's constitution is best described as...
options: a single codified document like the United States'
uncodified, drawn from statutes, rulings, and conventions
questions.explanation: The United Kingdom has an uncodified constitution spread across many sources rather than one document.

lessons.title: Executives: presidential and parliamentary systems
lessons.grammar_note: Keep 'head of state' and 'head of government' separate: in many parliamentary systems they are two people (a monarch or president plus a prime minister), while in a presidential system one person is usually both.

sections.heading: What you'll be able to do
sections.text: You will be able to contrast presidential, parliamentary, and semi-presidential systems, and explain how each handles the relationship between the executive and the legislature. Warm-up: in a parliamentary system, what happens to the government if it loses the legislature's confidence?

sections.heading: The idea
sections.text: The executive is the branch that carries out laws and runs day-to-day government. Systems differ mainly in how the executive relates to the legislature. In a presidential system, voters elect the president separately from the legislature for a fixed term; the president is both head of state and head of government and cannot normally be removed by a simple legislative vote. This is a separation of powers with mutual checks. In a parliamentary system, the executive emerges from the legislature: the prime minister and cabinet hold office only while they keep the confidence of the majority, and they can be removed by a vote of no confidence. The head of state (a monarch or ceremonial president) is a separate, largely symbolic figure. A semi-presidential system blends the two, pairing a directly elected president with a prime minister who answers to the legislature. Each design trades off stability, accountability, and the risk of deadlock differently.

sections.heading: Concepts and country examples
sections.text: The United States is the classic presidential system: the president and Congress are elected separately and can belong to different parties, producing checks but also the risk of gridlock. The United Kingdom and Germany are parliamentary: the prime minister or chancellor leads the majority in the legislature, and in Germany a 'constructive vote of no confidence' lets parliament remove a chancellor only by simultaneously electing a successor, which adds stability. In the United Kingdom the monarch is head of state while the prime minister governs. France is semi-presidential: a directly elected president shares power with a prime minister accountable to the National Assembly, and when the two come from opposing camps the result is called cohabitation. Presidential systems tend to give clear, fixed-term leadership but can stall when branches clash; parliamentary systems fuse the branches, easing lawmaking but letting governments fall between scheduled elections.

sections.heading: Your turn
sections.text: 1) Who is both head of state and head of government in a presidential system? 2) How can a parliamentary legislature remove the executive? 3) What makes a system semi-presidential? 4) What is Germany's constructive vote of no confidence? 5) What is French cohabitation? Answers: 1) the president. 2) by a vote of no confidence. 3) a directly elected president shares power with a prime minister accountable to the legislature. 4) parliament can oust a chancellor only by electing a replacement at the same time. 5) when the president and prime minister come from opposing political camps.

sections.heading: Common mistakes and exit ticket
sections.text: Mistake: assuming every country with a president is a presidential system; France has a president yet is semi-presidential, and some presidents are purely ceremonial. Mistake: thinking a prime minister serves a fixed term like a president; prime ministers hold office only while they keep majority confidence. Exit ticket: (a) Name the mechanism that removes a government in a parliamentary system. (b) Which country is the standard example of a presidential system? Answers: a vote of no confidence; the United States.

lessons.title: Legislatures, electoral systems, and parties
lessons.grammar_note: 'FPTP' (first-past-the-post) describes how votes become seats, while 'two-party system' describes the result; the electoral rule is a cause and the party system is largely an effect.

sections.heading: What you'll be able to do
sections.text: You will be able to describe what legislatures do, contrast first-past-the-post with proportional representation, and connect electoral rules to the number of parties a country tends to have. Warm-up: why might the same share of votes give a party very different numbers of seats under different rules?

sections.heading: The idea
sections.text: A legislature makes laws, approves budgets, and holds the executive to account; many are bicameral, with two chambers. How its seats are filled shapes the whole political landscape. Under first-past-the-post (FPTP), the country is divided into single-member districts and whoever gets the most votes in each district wins the seat, even without a majority. This rewards large, geographically concentrated parties and tends, over time, toward two-party competition, a regularity known as Duverger's law. Under proportional representation (PR), seats are allocated to parties in proportion to their vote share, usually in multi-member districts, which lets smaller parties win seats and typically produces multiparty systems and coalition governments. Mixed systems combine both. The resulting party system, meaning how many parties seriously compete and how they relate, follows largely from these rules, though social divisions and history matter too.

sections.heading: Concepts and country examples
sections.text: The United States and the United Kingdom use first-past-the-post and have long been dominated by two major parties, the Democrats and Republicans and the Conservatives and Labour respectively, though smaller parties persist. Germany uses mixed-member proportional representation: voters cast one vote for a local candidate and one for a party list, and an overall proportional outcome yields a multiparty Bundestag that usually governs by coalition. The Netherlands and Israel use highly proportional systems with low thresholds, producing many parties. France elects its National Assembly by a two-round majority system, which can squeeze smaller parties in the runoff. Party systems are described by their number: dominant-party, two-party, and multiparty. None is simply better; FPTP tends to give single-party majorities and clear accountability, while PR tends to give broad representation and coalition bargaining. The choice embeds a trade-off between decisiveness and inclusiveness.

sections.heading: Your turn
sections.text: 1) Under FPTP, how many winners are there per district? 2) What does proportional representation try to match? 3) What does Duverger's law predict? 4) Name a country that uses mixed-member proportional representation. 5) What trade-off separates FPTP from PR? Answers: 1) one, the candidate with the most votes. 2) each party's seat share to its vote share. 3) that FPTP tends to produce a two-party system. 4) Germany. 5) FPTP favors decisive single-party majorities; PR favors broad, inclusive representation through coalitions.

sections.heading: Common mistakes and exit ticket
sections.text: Mistake: assuming FPTP requires a majority; it needs only a plurality, the most votes, not more than half. Mistake: treating electoral rules as neutral plumbing; they systematically favor some kinds of parties over others. Exit ticket: (a) Which rule tends toward two parties? (b) Which tends toward multiparty coalitions? Answers: first-past-the-post; proportional representation.

lessons.title: Political economy and political change
lessons.grammar_note: 'Policy' is a chosen course of government action, while 'politics' is the contest over who decides; good analysis keeps the outcome (policy) separate from the struggle that produced it (politics).

sections.heading: What you'll be able to do
sections.text: You will be able to explain what political economy studies, describe how states shape markets and welfare, and distinguish revolution from gradual democratization. Warm-up: name one way governments differ in how much they intervene in the economy.

sections.heading: The idea
sections.text: Political economy studies how political power and economic life shape each other: who gets what, how markets are governed, and how states tax, spend, and regulate. Comparativists contrast market economies, where prices and private firms drive most decisions, with command economies, where the state plans production, and note that every real system mixes the two. Welfare states, which pool risk through pensions, health care, and unemployment support, come in different models, from more market-oriented to more comprehensive. Public policy is the chosen course of government action in a given area. Political change is the other half of the story. Some change is gradual, through reform and elections; some is abrupt. A revolution is a rapid, fundamental transformation of a state and its social order, often by force. Democratization is the slower shift from authoritarian toward democratic rule, which can advance or reverse.

sections.heading: Concepts and country examples
sections.text: Scholars describe 'varieties of capitalism', contrasting liberal market economies such as the United States and the United Kingdom, which rely heavily on open markets, with coordinated market economies such as Germany, which lean more on negotiation among firms, unions, and banks. France has historically featured a strong state role in the economy. China combines one-party rule with large, state-guided markets, a distinctive mix. On change, the French Revolution of 1789 and the Russian Revolution of 1917 are classic cases of abrupt, violent transformation. The political scientist Samuel Huntington described democratization arriving in 'waves', including the spread of democracy in southern Europe and Latin America in the 1970s and 1980s and across parts of Eastern Europe after 1989. Transitions are not guaranteed to stick; backsliding, where elected leaders erode checks on their power, is a recognized risk studied across many countries.

sections.heading: Your turn
sections.text: 1) What does political economy study? 2) What is the difference between a market and a command economy? 3) Define a revolution in one line. 4) What did Huntington mean by waves of democratization? 5) What is democratic backsliding? Answers: 1) how political power and economic life shape each other. 2) in a market economy prices and private firms decide; in a command economy the state plans production. 3) a rapid, fundamental transformation of a state and its social order. 4) clusters of countries becoming democratic around the same period. 5) the erosion of checks on power, often by elected leaders, moving a democracy toward authoritarian rule.

sections.heading: Common mistakes and exit ticket
sections.text: Mistake: equating any protest or coup with a revolution; a revolution transforms the basic order, not just the office-holders. Mistake: assuming democratization is permanent once it begins; transitions can stall or reverse. Exit ticket: (a) Contrast a liberal and a coordinated market economy. (b) Name one historical revolution. Answers: liberal market economies rely mainly on open markets (United States, United Kingdom), while coordinated ones rely more on negotiation among firms, unions, and banks (Germany); the French Revolution of 1789 or the Russian Revolution of 1917.

items.translation: a state's claim to supreme authority over a territory and its people
items.example: A sovereign state answers to no higher power within its own borders.

items.translation: the widely held belief that those who govern have the right to do so
items.example: A government that wins fair elections usually enjoys broad legitimacy.

items.translation: a system that concentrates power and limits competition, but not every part of life
items.example: An authoritarian regime may allow private business while banning opposition parties.

items.translation: a system in which a constitution divides power between national and regional governments
items.example: Under federalism, German Lander hold powers the central government cannot simply remove.

items.translation: an electoral rule in which the candidate with the most votes in a district wins the single seat
items.example: First-past-the-post helped produce two dominant parties in the United Kingdom.

items.translation: an electoral rule that allocates seats to parties in proportion to their vote share
items.example: Proportional representation gives small parties in the Netherlands a realistic path to seats.

items.translation: the process of moving from authoritarian toward democratic rule

questions.prompt: In a presidential system, the president is removed from office by...
options: a routine vote of no confidence
not easily; the president serves a fixed term barring exceptional removal
questions.explanation: A president serves a fixed term and is not subject to an ordinary confidence vote, unlike a prime minister.

questions.prompt: France's system, pairing a directly elected president with a prime minister answerable to the legislature, is called...
questions.explanation: Semi-presidential systems combine an elected president with a prime minister accountable to parliament.

questions.prompt: Duverger's law links first-past-the-post elections to...
questions.explanation: Single-member plurality rules tend, over time, to favor two large parties.

questions.prompt: Germany's electoral system for the Bundestag is best described as...
questions.explanation: German voters cast a district vote and a party-list vote, yielding an overall proportional, multiparty result.

questions.prompt: A coordinated market economy, such as Germany's, relies comparatively more on...
options: negotiation among firms, unions, and banks
questions.explanation: Coordinated market economies emphasize negotiation among economic actors, versus the market reliance of liberal economies.

questions.prompt: Democratic backsliding refers to...
options: a revolution that overthrows the state
the gradual erosion of checks on power, often by elected leaders
questions.explanation: Backsliding is the weakening of democratic constraints from within, moving a system toward authoritarian rule.
